title: Basic operations on explicit sets
statements: B and C are disjoint sets.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A ∩ B = {3, 4, 5}.**  (true)

The elements common to both A and B are 3, 4, and 5.

**B) A ∪ C = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}.**  (false)

Trap: A contributes 1–5, C contributes 5–9, so together they cover every integer from 1 to 9 — the statement's set stops at 8 and wrongly omits 9, which C contributes.

**C) (A ∩ B) ∩ C = {5}.**  (true)

A ∩ B = {3,4,5}; intersecting this with C = {5,6,7,8,9} leaves only the common element 5.

**D) A \ C = {1, 2, 3}.**  (false)

A \ C removes from A any elements that are also in C. Only 5 is in both, so A \ C = {1,2,3,4} — the statement is missing the element 4.

**E) B and C are disjoint sets.**  (false)

B and C share the elements 5, 6, and 7, so they are not disjoint (disjoint would require B ∩ C = ). ∅

Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, B = {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}, and C = {5, 6, 7, 8, 9}.

Compute the key sets once: A ∩ B = {3, 4, 5}; A C covers 1–5 (from A) and 5–9 (from C) ∪ with no gaps, so A C = {1,...,9}; A \ C removes only the shared element 5, leaving {1,2,3,4}; and B ∩ C = ∪ {5,6,7} (nonempty, so B and C are NOT disjoint). **4.** (FALSE) A \ C = {1, 2, 3}.

**5.** (FALSE) B and C are disjoint sets.

**A) The power set of A has 8 elements.**  (true)

A set with 3 elements has 2³ = 8 subsets in total, so its power set contains 8 elements.

**B) {a, b} is an element of A.**  (false)

The elements of A are a, b, and c individually. {a,b} is a subset of A, not an element of A — confusing “element of” with “subset of” is a common mistake.

**C) ∅ is a subset of A.**  (true)

The empty set is a subset of every set, including A.

**D) A is a proper subset of A.**  (false)

A proper subset must be strictly smaller than the original set (not equal to it). Since A = A, A is not a proper subset of itself.

**E) There are exactly 3 subsets of A that contain exactly 2 elements.**  (true)

The 2-element subsets are {a,b}, {a,c}, and {b,c} — exactly three of them.

Let A = {a, b, c}.

title: Let E = {1, 3, 5, 7} and F = {3, 4, 5, 6}.
statements: E \ F = F \ E
tactical_explanations:
**A) E \ F = {1, 7}**  (true)

Removing from E every element also found in F (3 and 5) leaves {1, 7}.

**B) F \ E = {4, 6}**  (true)

Removing from F every element also found in E (3 and 5) leaves {4, 6}.

**C) E \ F = F \ E**  (false)

Trap: set difference is NOT commutative in general. E \ F = {1,7} while F \ E = {4,6} — these are different sets, so the equality fails.

**D) (E \ F) (F \ E) = {1, 4, 6, 7} ∪**  (true)

The union of the two "one-sided" differences, {1,7} {4,6} = {1,4,6,7}, is exactly the symmetric ∪ difference E F: the elements belonging to exactly one of the two sets. △

**E) (E \ F) ∩ (F \ E) = ∅**  (true)

By construction, E \ F contains only elements outside F, and F \ E contains only elements outside E, so the two sets can never share an element — their intersection is always empty.

**5.** (TRUE) (E \ F) ∩ (F \ E) = ∅

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

title: Partitions of a set
context: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. A partition of A is a collection of nonempty, pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is A.
statements: P = { {1,2}, {3,4}, {5,6} } is a partition of A.
Every partition of a set must have exactly the same number of blocks as the set has elements.
Q = { {1,2,3}, {3,4,5,6} } is a partition of A.
R = { {1,2}, {3,4}, {5} } is a partition of A.
A set with n ≥ 2 elements always has more than one possible partition.
tactical_explanations:
**A) P = { {1,2}, {3,4}, {5,6} } is a partition of A.**  (true)

The three blocks are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, and their union {1,2,3,4,5,6} equals A — all partition requirements are satisfied.

**B) Every partition of a set must have exactly the same number of blocks as the set has elements.**  (false)

A partition can have any number of blocks, from 1 (the whole set as a single block) up to n (all singletons) — there's no requirement that the number of blocks equals |A|, as (a) already shows with 3 blocks for 6 elements.

**C) Q = { {1,2,3}, {3,4,5,6} } is a partition of A.**  (false)

The blocks {1,2,3} and {3,4,5,6} both contain the element 3, violating the requirement that blocks be pairwise disjoint.

**D) R = { {1,2}, {3,4}, {5} } is a partition of A.**  (false)

The union of R's blocks is {1,2,3,4,5}, which misses the element 6 — the blocks don't cover all of A.

**E) A set with n ≥ 2 elements always has more than one possible partition.**  (true)

For any n ≥ 2, at least two distinct partitions always exist — for example, the single block {A} itself, and the partition into all singletons — and these are different whenever n ≥ 2.
solution_overview:
Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. A partition of A is a collection of nonempty, pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is A.

**Part 1: Setup.**

A valid partition needs blocks that are (1) nonempty, (2) pairwise disjoint, and (3) collectively cover every element of A exactly once. Check each candidate against all three: P={{1,2},{3,4},{5,6}} passes; Q fails disjointness (3 appears twice); R fails coverage (misses 6). There's no rule tying the number of blocks to |A|.

**Part 2: Check each claim.**

**1.** (TRUE) P = { {1,2}, {3,4}, {5,6} } is a partition of A.

**2.** (FALSE) Every partition of a set must have exactly the same number of blocks as the set has elements.

**3.** (FALSE) Q = { {1,2,3}, {3,4,5,6} } is a partition of A.

**4.** (FALSE) R = { {1,2}, {3,4}, {5} } is a partition of A.

**5.** (TRUE) A set with n ≥ 2 elements always has more than one possible partition.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

title: Counting subsets
context: Let A be a set with |A| = 5. ===== PAGE 10 =====
statements: The number of subsets of A is 32.
The number of proper subsets of A is 31.
The number of subsets of A containing exactly 4 elements is 10.
The number of nonempty subsets of A is 31.
The number of subsets of A containing an even number of elements (0, 2, or 4) is 15.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of subsets of A is 32.**  (true)

A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets; here 2⁵ = 32.

**B) The number of proper subsets of A is 31.**  (true)

A proper subset excludes only A itself, so 32 − 1 = 31 subsets qualify.

**C) The number of subsets of A containing exactly 4 elements is 10.**  (false)

The number of 4-element subsets is C(5,4) = 5, not 10 (10 is actually the count for 3-element or 2- element subsets, C(5,3)=C(5,2)=10 — a mismatch with the wrong size here).

**D) The number of nonempty subsets of A is 31.**  (true)

Excluding only the empty set from the 32 total subsets leaves 32 − 1 = 31 nonempty subsets.

**E) The number of subsets of A containing an even number of elements (0, 2, or 4) is 15.**  (false)

Summing C(5,0)+C(5,2)+C(5,4) = 1+10+5 = 16, not 15 — the actual count of even-sized subsets is 16.
solution_overview:
Let A be a set with |A| = 5. ===== PAGE 10 =====

**Part 1: Setup.**
